case_study_insert.main_stem: Preston Premier Leisure (PPL) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, running a fitness and leisure club with a workforce of 70. Founded in 1998 by Chloe Grant, the business operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. PPL plans to invest $420,000 in a gym extension with a swimming pool and smart-access technology, financed by a $250,000 ten-year bank loan and a $170,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $44, and currently produces 15,000 units a year. PPL faces two problems: equipment breakdown downtime has risen and staff absenteeism has reached 9%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: PPL recorded 3,800 member visits last quarter with an equipment-fault rate of 4.1%, down from 6.3% a year ago. Member complaints fell from 55 to 27 per month. Average queue time at reception is 4.5 minutes. A survey of 650 gym members found that 69% would pay $18 more for the new pool and smart-access facilities and 58% choose a gym on equipment reliability. A training audit shows 22 of 70 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the smart-access system; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Preston Premier Leisure for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.5% to 4.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.77 to $13.60 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Gym equipment and energy input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, while consumer spending on fitness and leisure grew 4.7% in the same period.

questions.question_text: PPL plans to fund part of its $420,000 gym extension with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for PPL of using a share issue to raise the $170,000 instead of extra bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share capital needs no interest or capital repayment, protecting PPL's cash flow while it already carries a $250,000 bank loan and fixed costs of $210,000 a year. That helps absorb the 10.2% rise in equipment and energy costs without raising the $44 member-visit price.

Point 2: Equity spreads the risk of the new pool and smart-access facilities among shareholders, so the club is not exposed to loan covenants or repossession if visitor numbers miss the 15,000 target. It also enlarges the capital base supporting the $420,000 investment without increasing the interest payable already shown in Appendix 2.

Equity also fits a long-lived asset: the pool and smart-access system should lift member visits over many years, so funding the whole $420,000 with ten-year loan interest would mismatch costs and benefits. A share issue keeps the $250,000 bank loan as the only debt and leaves the $18 premium and 69% willingness-to-pay to drive revenue without an extra repayment schedule. That resilience matters while the 4.1% equipment-fault rate and 9% absenteeism are being tackled.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over bank borrowing (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PPL's expansion, loan and cost data.

questions.question_text: PPL is launching its new pool and smart-access facilities. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should PPL choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television: A national TV campaign would showcase the new pool to a mass audience quickly, but airtime is very costly for a 70-staff club funding a $420,000 extension, and most viewers are outside the local catchment, so spending would be largely wasted.

Local radio: Regional radio is cheap and reaches Preston households near the club, ideal for time-limited launch offers. Its weakness is narrow reach and no visuals of the smart-access facilities, which may not bring in the 15,000 visits needed to cover $210,000 of fixed costs.

Social media influencer marketing: Fitness and lifestyle influencers reach exactly the 69% of 650 surveyed members who would pay $18 more for the pool and smart-access facilities and the 58% who choose on equipment reliability. It is measurable, nationally scalable and low cost per lead, though results build gradually and depend on influencer credibility.

PPL's 2025 operating profit is $630,000, yet a national TV spot would still be poor value because most viewers lie outside the Preston catchment; influencer spend can be capped and measured against the $30 contribution per visit and 3,800 visits last quarter. Local radio cannot show the pool, and its 4.5-minute queue message lacks visual impact. A targeted digital campaign fits a 70-staff club and the 69% willingness to pay found in the survey.

Recommendation: PPL should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the exact survey segment, shows the facilities visually and costs far less than television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; local radio is rejected as too narrow and non-visual, so PPL should add member referral incentives to convert the interest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to PPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PPL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in PPL's context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: PPL's equipment breakdown downtime has risen and staff absenteeism has reached 9%. Explain two benefits for PPL of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets PPL's 70 staff contribute ideas on maintaining the new pool and smart-access system, raising ownership and job satisfaction. Staff who help set maintenance routines are more likely to report faults early, cutting the 4.1% equipment-fault rate and the rising breakdown downtime.

Point 2: Involving reception and gym teams in decisions improves service quality and cuts the queue time and member complaints, supporting the 58% who choose on reliability. Higher involvement reduces the 9% absenteeism and staff turnover, avoiding repeated $950 per employee retraining and protecting the 15,000-visit target.

Democratic leadership suits a 70-staff club where reception and gym teams spot faults first; their input can reduce the 4.1% equipment-fault rate and the rising downtime that drives the 58% reliability choice. Better morale cuts the 9% absenteeism and the $950 retraining cycle, protecting the 43.0% gross margin and the 15,000 visits needed to service the $420,000 extension. Stable staff also shorten the 4.5-minute reception queue and cut member complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PPL's downtime, absenteeism and output.

questions.question_text: PPL must upskill 22 staff to operate the new smart-access system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should PPL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Demonstrations on PPL's own smart-access system are directly relevant, cost no fees and keep all 22 staff on duty, protecting the 3,800 member visits recorded last quarter and the fall in faults to 4.1%. Drawbacks are that trainer-staff lose time, mistakes may be copied and no formal certificate is given.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $950 per employee gives structured skills and a recognised certificate for 22 staff, costing $20,900 - modest beside the $420,000 extension. It withdraws 22 of 70 staff from the club, raising queue times, and generic content may not match PPL's system, so on-site follow-up would be needed.

The 22 staff are about 31% of the 70-strong workforce, so a full college course would remove a third of front-of-house capacity and lengthen the 4.5-minute queue at launch. On-the-job coaching on the actual smart-access system keeps all 22 on duty and protects the 3,800-visit quarter. PPL should still record competence checks for security and quality, and can add short college modules from the 15.0% operating margin if certification later becomes necessary.

Decision: PPL should choose on-the-job training, with short college modules for senior staff. It is cheaper, system-specific and avoids losing front-of-house capacity while absenteeism is 9%; full off-the-job training is rejected because a $20,900 fee and 22 staff away would lengthen the 4.5-minute reception queue and worsen complaints, and college sessions can be added once the system is stable.

A $20,900 single-cohort fee would eat into the $420,000 extension budget, while on-the-job coaching can be repeated for new staff at no further cost.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to PPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in PPL's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in PPL's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and system relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PPL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($44 − $14) = $210,000 ÷ $30 = 7,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 7,000 member visits a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $44 − $14 = $30. Answer: contribution per unit is $30.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PPL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 7,000-visit break-even point with 15,000 actual visits, a margin of safety of 8,000, to judge whether the new pool is justified.
2. Use $30 contribution to test a $6 off-peak discount to $38, leaving $24 per visit, still above the $14 variable cost while filling quiet periods.
3. Set visit targets that service the $250,000 bank loan and justify the $420,000 extension before Chloe Grant commits further capital.
4. Track average total cost of $28.0 ($210,000 ÷ 15,000 + $14) each quarter to spot downtime waste and to check whether the 10.2% energy and equipment-cost rise is being absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 7,000 visits | (ii) Contribution per unit = $30 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety vs 15,000 visits; discount modelling vs $210,000 fixed costs; loan servicing for the $420,000 extension; and average total cost of $28.0 to monitor energy inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid, contextual use in (iii) (max 4).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PPL's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has PPL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 43.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $1,440,000 on revenue of $3,600,000 is 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $1,806,000 on revenue of $4,200,000 is 43.0%. Operating profit of $432,000 in 2024 equals 12.0% of revenue and 18.0% of the $2,400,000 capital employed; in 2025 operating profit of $630,000 is 15.0% of revenue and 22.5% of the $2,800,000 capital employed. Cost of sales rose from $2,160,000 to $2,394,000 but more slowly than revenue.

Evaluation: All three measures moved favourably. Gross margins widened from 40.0% to 43.0%, suggesting better control of energy and maintenance costs; operating margins rose from 12.0% to 15.0%, so more of each visit fee becomes operating profit; and returns on capital employed increased from 18.0% to 22.5%, showing the asset base is working harder. Interest payable rose from $40,000 to $52,000, a growing but small burden, and a 10.2% energy-cost rise could erode the gross-margin gain.

Interest payable of $52,000 remains small against $630,000 operating profit, so debt service does not overturn the improvement, though the 10.2% energy-cost rise needs monitoring to protect the enlarged 43.0% margin.

Conclusion: PPL's financial position has improved on every permitted measure, and because margins and capital returns both rose the improvement is not simply a revenue effect. The main risk is rising interest and energy costs, so management should defend the 43.0% gross margin before the $420,000 extension loads more capital into the club.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of margin, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PPL of offering the $18 premium for the new pool and smart-access facilities identified in its member survey.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Of 650 members surveyed, 69% would pay $18 more for the pool and smart-access facilities and 58% choose on equipment reliability, so the premium lifts revenue per visit and protects the $30 contribution even as energy and equipment costs rise 10.2%. It also reinforces PPL's modern club brand.

Disadvantage: Price-sensitive members may reject the $18 premium, cutting the 15,000 visits needed to justify the $420,000 extension and worsening the equipment downtime if maintenance is deferred. A failed smart-access system could also raise the 4.1% equipment-fault rate and the 9% absenteeism, undermining reliability.

PPL should trial the $18 premium on the new pool and measure take-up against the 69% who said they would pay, because the 58% reliability segment expects the smart-access system to work. A two-tier fee could alienate existing members and reduce the 15,000 visits required for the $250,000 loan, so part of the premium should fund maintenance and the $950 staff training. That reinvestment defends the 43.0% gross margin instead of merely harvesting it.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PPL's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in gym equipment and energy input costs will affect PPL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.5% to 4.25%): If PPL's $250,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $250,000 = $1,875 a year, modest beside $210,000 of fixed costs; a fixed loan removes even that. Higher rates may reduce discretionary leisure spending and raise future borrowing costs, which PPL can limit by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.60 an hour): With a workforce of 70, reception and support roles are hourly-paid, so the wage bill rises and is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours or pay rates, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity - 15,000 visits ÷ 70 staff = about 214 visits per worker - meaning the rise is absorbable only if that productivity holds, or the $30 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (10.2%): The $14 variable cost per visit covers energy and equipment consumables, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: a full 10.2% rise is 0.102 × $14 = $1.43 per visit, about $21,420 a year at 15,000 visits (15,000 × $1.43). Even a partial rise cuts contribution, and the $18 premium offsets only part.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in equipment and energy costs has the greatest impact because it touches all 15,000 visits and directly erodes the $30 contribution funding the $420,000 extension; the wage rise is manageable at about 214 visits per worker, and the interest rise costs at most $1,875 and can be fixed, so neither matches the input-cost shock.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to PPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on PPL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in PPL's context with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
